---
title: "A3 — Gas exchange and circulation"
---

## Follow oxygen all the way to a working cell

During increased activity, muscle ATP demand rises. Breathing faster is only
one possible response. Oxygen must reach the respiratory surface, cross a
barrier, enter an internal transport system where needed, leave that system
near the tissue and reach mitochondria. This unit follows that pathway and
connects ventilation, exchange surfaces, blood and the pump.

By the end, explain diffusion and bulk flow as different processes; compare
fish, mammalian and insect gas transport; interpret oxygen content separately
from partial pressure; trace mammalian circulation; and connect vessel and
respiratory histology to function. Work through the [slides](lec.qmd),
[exercises](exercise.qmd) and [quiz](quiz.qmd).

## Diffusion needs a gradient and a suitable barrier

A gas diffuses according to differences in its chemical potential, commonly
described in physiology using partial pressure. **Partial pressure** is the
pressure contribution of one gas in a mixture. A gas in solution also has
an associated partial pressure related to dissolved, unbound gas. Oxygen
can have the same partial pressure in two fluids while their total oxygen
contents differ greatly because one contains an oxygen-binding pigment.

For a simple barrier, transfer rate increases with area and the partial-pressure
difference and decreases with barrier thickness. We can write the proportional
relationship as $\dot M \propto A\Delta P/L$, holding the material's diffusion
properties constant. Doubling area doubles predicted transfer; doubling
thickness halves it. This is a simplified comparison, because actual respiratory
surfaces also have flow, varying gradients and heterogeneous structure.

Thinness and large area bring costs. A delicate moist surface needs protection,
and a surface exposed to air can lose water. A respiratory organ must therefore
combine exchange efficiency with support, protection and ventilation. In
mammalian lung tissue, thin alveolar walls and nearby capillaries shorten the
route between air and blood. Larger airways have a different task: conducting
air, with supporting and protective structures rather than gas exchange across
their full walls. See the openly accessible overview of
[exchange systems](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/39-1-systems-of-gas-exchange).

## Ventilation and perfusion renew the two sides

**Ventilation** moves environmental medium over a respiratory surface.
**Perfusion** supplies internal fluid, often blood, to that surface. Both
can maintain gradients by replacing fluid that has already exchanged gases.
Increasing one alone may do little if the other is severely limiting.

A fish gill presents a large thin area to water. Water and blood commonly move
in opposite directions across exchange regions. In an ideal countercurrent
arrangement, a gradient can persist along the exchange path, allowing more
complete extraction than a comparable co-current arrangement. It is not
necessary for oxygen to move “uphill”: at every exchange location the net
diffusion remains down a local partial-pressure gradient. Maintaining flow
and supporting the gill are themselves physiological tasks.

Mammalian lungs use tidal ventilation: air moves in and out along shared
conducting pathways. Fresh incoming air mixes with air already present, and
not every part of an inspired breath reaches exchange regions. Birds provide
a useful contrast: their rigid exchange lungs and air-sac ventilation support
a different flow arrangement. Avoid describing air sacs themselves as the main
gas-exchanging surface. The details of avian flow exceed this first explanation;
the key point is that lungs are not all built as mammalian alveolar sacs.

Insects provide a further contrast. Tracheae and finer tracheoles bring gases
close to tissues; ventilation and diffusion contribute to transport. Their
circulating haemolymph generally has a smaller role in oxygen transport than
vertebrate blood. This is an important counterexample to the claim that every
active animal requires a vertebrate-style blood oxygen pathway.

## Oxygen pressure, content and delivery

In many vertebrates, haemoglobin carries most blood oxygen. Dissolved oxygen
contributes to partial pressure; haemoglobin-bound oxygen greatly increases
content. **Saturation** is the fraction of available binding sites occupied,
whereas **oxygen content** is an amount per volume of blood. Neither is a
synonym for partial pressure. A blood sample can have a normal oxygen partial
pressure yet carry less total oxygen if it contains less haemoglobin.

Cooperative oxygen binding produces an S-shaped relationship between
haemoglobin saturation and oxygen partial pressure under typical conditions.
The relation supports loading at high partial pressure and unloading as
partial pressure falls in tissues. Temperature, pH and carbon dioxide influence
affinity, helping coordinate delivery with local conditions. A rightward shift
means lower affinity at a stated partial pressure; it does not mean oxygen
has disappeared from the system.

Carbon dioxide returns from tissues in several forms, including bicarbonate,
bound compounds and dissolved gas. Conversion between carbon dioxide and
bicarbonate connects gas transport with acid–base balance. Ventilation can
change carbon dioxide loss, but oxygen and carbon dioxide regulation should
not be collapsed into a single “more breathing is always better” rule.
The supporting reading distinguishes
[gas exchange and transport](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/39-2-gas-exchange-across-respiratory-surfaces).

For a simplified steady-state accounting, oxygen use equals blood flow
multiplied by the arterial–venous oxygen-content difference. If flow is
5 L min⁻¹, arterial content 200 mL O₂ L⁻¹ and venous content 150 mL O₂ L⁻¹,
oxygen use is $5(200-150)=250$ mL O₂ min⁻¹. The product uses content,
not oxygen partial pressure. The calculation is a whole-system balance and
requires representative measurements under the assumed conditions.

## A circuit needs pressure differences and valves

In mammalian circulation, the right heart sends blood towards the lungs and
the left heart sends blood towards systemic tissues. Trace the circuit:
systemic veins → right atrium → right ventricle → pulmonary arteries → lungs
→ pulmonary veins → left atrium → left ventricle → systemic arteries.
An artery carries blood away from the heart; a vein returns it. Oxygenation
does not define these vessel names.

```{mermaid}
flowchart LR
  V[Systemic veins] --> RH[Right heart]
  RH --> PA[Pulmonary arteries]
  PA --> L[Lung exchange]
  L --> PV[Pulmonary veins]
  PV --> LH[Left heart]
  LH --> SA[Systemic arteries]
  SA --> T[Tissue exchange]
  T --> V
```

This original circuit sketch shows direction, not anatomical position or the
relative size of its compartments.

Valves help prevent reverse flow as chamber pressures change. The ventricular
wall develops pressure, but pressure is not identical to flow. A simple
relation is flow $Q=\Delta P/R$, where $R$ is vascular resistance. With a
fixed pressure difference, higher resistance gives lower flow. Smooth muscle
can alter vessel calibre and distribute flow among tissues. Narrow vessels
have high resistance individually, yet many small vessels arranged in parallel
can support substantial total flow and a very large exchange area.

Arteries generally have walls suited to pressure and its fluctuations.
Capillaries provide short exchange paths. Veins can hold a substantial blood
volume at relatively low pressure, and return is influenced by pressure
gradients, surrounding muscle and valves in appropriate locations. An empty
or collapsed vessel in a section can look different from a blood-filled one;
describe wall layers and surrounding tissue before naming it.

## Comparative circuits and coordinated responses

A fish typically sends blood from its heart through gills and then systemic
tissues in a single circuit. Mammals separate pulmonary and systemic circuits
with a four-chambered heart. Other vertebrates have other arrangements,
including variable separation of blood streams. Open circulations move
haemolymph through vessels and body spaces; closed circulations keep the main
transport fluid within vessels. “Open” does not mean motionless, and “closed”
does not automatically identify the animal's metabolic rate. Compare the
actual route, pressure, control and exchange requirements. A useful overview
is the reading on
[circulatory organisation](https://openstax.org/books/biology-2e/pages/40-1-overview-of-the-circulatory-system).

At the onset of exercise, ventilation, cardiac activity and local vascular
responses can act together. Cardiac output is heart rate times stroke volume.
Increasing heart rate is only one way to change output, and a measured rate
alone does not establish how much blood or oxygen reaches a tissue. Local
metabolites and neural/endocrine signals help coordinate supply and demand.

Explain an exercise response by naming each link: ATP demand changes;
tissue conditions change; ventilation and circulation respond; transport
and exchange change; the resulting tissue conditions influence the response.
Check whether your account confuses a pump action, a flow, a pressure, a gas
content or a diffusion gradient. Continue to
[water, ions and excretion](../water-excretion/index.qmd).
